First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph.
  Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs.
  Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

items.title: L2C2: Enhancing Large-scale Chiplets for Agent Long-Context LLM Inference with Sparse and Distributed Attention
items.raw_content:
Authors: Kangbo Bai, Zhonghua Mu, Hongze Zhou, Tianyu Jia

Long-context inference is a rising demand for LLMs, especially for agent applications. Sparse attention (SpAt) and chiplet technology are promising solutions to reduce computations and scale hardware performance. However, deploying SpAt on distributed chiplets necessitates context parallelism for workload partitioning, introducing complex distributed attention. In this work, we present L2C2, a system optimization for distributed SpAt in long-context inference. During the partial-prefill stage, we propose a novel Split-Comm Attention mechanism that leverages the high-bandwidth interconnect of chiplets to trade communication overhead for reduced memory access. We combine it with conventional Ring Attention to form a Bi-Mode method that adapts to varying input sequence lengths. During the decoding stage, we analyze the cause of memory access imbalance and address it by static interleaved token assignment. Dynamic agile cache balancing is also proposed to adapt to SpAt skewness. Evaluations show our optimization can achieve 1.45$\times$ and 1.53$\times$ speedup in partial-prefill and decoding with SpAt on large-scale chiplets.

items.title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys
items.raw_content:
Authors: Yongkang Xiao, Jing Chen, Min Shi, Kun He, Mei Wang et al.

Modern cryptographic protocols such as WPA2-PSK, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Bluetooth Classic (BC) tolerate low-entropy keys for user-friendliness, backward compatibility, or resource-constrained deployment, yet existing symbolic protocol verifiers rely on the perfect-encryption assumption and therefore cannot reason about brute-force attackers. Prior work addresses this gap only through protocol-specific, manually encoded reveal rules, which neither generalize across protocols nor systematically explore compound-key decomposition. We introduce the first protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic methodology for low-entropy keys, built on three abstractions: the message-derivation fact MDerive, which captures brute-force prerequisites independently of concrete function symbols; a three-tier breaking-oracle design (value-breaking, relationship-breaking, message-derivation) that composes with the standard Dolev-Yao attacker; and a graded bit-level attacker model that bounds the key length an attacker is allowed to exhaust. We realize the methodology as EntropyVerif, a syntax-sugar extension of Tamarin that requires no kernel modification. Using EntropyVerif we automatically rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks, and uncover a new attack on BC which we call the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack: by repeatedly downgrading one side of a BC session and recombining the recovered key fragments, an attacker reduces session-key recovery against devices using the maximum 128-bit key from $2^{128}$ to $n \cdot 2^{128/n}$, bottoming out at $2^{12}$ for $n=16$---a factor of $2^{116}$ reduction that has been responsibly disclosed to the Bluetooth SIG. Across three real-world protocols and six BC device configurations, our results show that entropy-aware symbolic analysis is both feasible and necessary.

items.title: Algebraic Diversity of Switching Functions
items.raw_content:
Authors: Mitchell A. Thornton

Algebraic Diversity generalizes averaging over many observations to averaging one observation over a group of transformations matched to its structure. This paper develops the framework on the Boolean cube $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for the translations, the coordinate permutations, the hyperoctahedral group, and the general linear and affine groups. It determines the commutant of each action and gives closed forms for the group-averaged second-order statistic of one truth table, which collapses to the Walsh periodogram for the translations, to per-weight averages for the hyperoctahedral group, and to the weight up to complementation for the affine group. Bent functions are exactly those whose translation average is white, the Haar transform along an input order is the multiplexer tree of Shannon's expansion, and higher-order averages see only the weight below a first informative order, two for the translations and four for the affine group. A matched stabilizer stands in for repeated observations, since a vote over orbits of $s$ points divides by $s$ the number of noisy truth tables a target error requires. The same viewpoint gives the affine hull of a function as matched coordinates, an exact variance identity for XOR hashing, and matched hashes whose variance never exceeds that of a pairwise independent hash. Applications on public benchmarks include hash choice for approximate model counting, the decision of parity-structured formulas and the refutation of counting formulas modulo 3 and 4 from the spectra of clause blocks, separation of NPN classes by canonical spectra, tested on ISCAS-85 cut functions and all five-input classes, correction of noisy truth tables and protection of lookup tables by voting over symmetries, blind group matching, and an analog of the CLEAN algorithm that writes a truth table as the XOR of atoms in the fixed spaces of groups. All proofs are given in full.

items.title: DiversePlace: Diversity-Seeking Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Macro Placement
items.raw_content:
Authors: Wenrui Zhou, Jiashun Liu, Wenji Fang, Zhiyao Xie, Ling Pan

Macro placement is a critical early-stage decision in physical design because macro locations strongly constrain subsequent implementation stages. The task is difficult because these high-impact discrete decisions must be made before downstream quality can be measured accurately, forcing training to rely on fast but imperfect training-time oracles such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL). Existing RL-based placers therefore mostly optimize single HPWL-driven solutions, and their long sequential horizons often require heavy search assistance or offline expert data while leaving little room to preserve multiple competitive layouts. We address this gap by making quality-controlled diversity an explicit objective for macro placement. Instead of relying on a single proxy-optimal solution, we maintain a compact archive of HPWL-competitive yet meaningfully different placements for downstream selection. We realize this idea in DiversePlace, a curriculum proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that combines a quality-gated diversity reward with an expanding placement horizon, enabling from-scratch RL optimization while keeping exploration inside competitive HPWL regions. On the ISPD2005 benchmarks, DiversePlace consistently improves top-5, top-10, and top-20 archive diversity and achieves lower or virtually identical HPWL on all eight designs with better efficiency. Code: https://github.com/William030422/NIPS2026-DiversePlace.

items.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
items.raw_content:
Authors: Yaser Kord, Moritz Hess

Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.

items.title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth
items.raw_content:
Authors: Anthony Mikhaiel, Essam Ghadafi

Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $μ$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.

items.title: From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
items.raw_content:
Authors: Mehran Moghadam, Abu Masum, M. Hassan Najafi, Sercan Aygun, Di Wu

Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.

items.title: GPS: Guiding Phase-Level Prefetcher Selection with Data-Driven Method
items.raw_content:
Authors: Buqing Xu, Mengming Li, Qijun Zhang, Ziyan Guo, Zhiyao Xie

Hardware prefetching is a widely used technique for hiding off-chip memory latency. Modern processors increasingly adopt composite prefetchers that combine multiple prefetching engines to handle the diverse memory access patterns found in real applications. However, coordinating multiple prefetchers requires a policy selection algorithm that maps observed system feedback to appropriate prefetching policies. Existing approaches suffer from two key limitations. First, relying on only a small set of features can lead to misleading prefetcher policies due to incomplete visibility into the system state. Second, limited on-chip hardware resources force these designs to use simple mapping mechanisms that cannot effectively navigate the large prefetching policy space.
  To address these challenges, we propose GPS, a data-driven framework for prefetcher selection that leverages comprehensive profiling and offline learning. GPS collects a rich set of features that capture both system behaviors and hardware resource states, and uses an offline machine learning model to learn the mapping between these features and the IPC-best policy. By offloading complex policy generation to software, GPS eliminates the need for costly online exploration and enables lightweight runtime execution through pre-generated policy hints. GPS reduces the performance gap to only 2.6%, compared to 13.6% and 14.2% in prior state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate GPS on SPEC CPU2006, SPEC CPU2017, and GAP benchmark suites. GPS outperforms the state-of-the-art prefetcher selection method I-POP by 12.14%, 8.34%, and 14.17% in geometric-mean IPC, respectively. GPS achieves these gains with only 778 bits of additional on-chip storage for runtime policy control.

items.title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery
items.raw_content:
Authors: Boyang Ma, Jinku Li, Hao Wu, Sheng Gao, Man Zhou et al.

LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.
